solution:
The **photoelectric effect** is the phenomenon of **emission of electrons from a metal surface when radiation of appropriate frequency is incident on it**.

A surface that emits electrons in this way is called a **photosensitive surface**, and the electrons released are called **photoelectrons**. Photoelectrons are ordinary electrons; the name only records that they were set free by incident light.

A metal contains free electrons, but they are confined inside it and cannot escape through the surface unless enough energy is supplied to them to overcome the barrier that holds them in. Incident radiation supplies that energy, and the effect has two characteristic features:

1. Emission occurs **only if the frequency of the incident radiation exceeds a threshold frequency** \(\nu_0\), which is a property of the emitter metal. If \(\nu < \nu_0\), not a single electron is emitted, however intense the radiation may be. If \(\nu > \nu_0\), electrons are emitted however feeble the radiation is.
2. Emission is **instantaneous** - the photocurrent starts within about \(10^{-9}\) s of the light striking the surface, and stops the moment the radiation is cut off.

Which radiation counts as "appropriate" depends on the metal. For metals such as zinc, cadmium and magnesium, ultraviolet radiation is necessary, while for the alkali metals even visible radiation is sufficient.

The effect was discovered by **Heinrich Hertz in 1887**, who noticed that when ultraviolet light was incident on a metal electrode a high-voltage spark passed across the electrodes - electrons were in fact being emitted from the metal surface.

**No. Microwaves cannot be used to produce the photoelectric effect.**

An electron is emitted only if the photon that strikes it carries at least the work function of the metal, i.e. only if \(h\nu \ge \phi_0\). The whole question is therefore whether a microwave photon is energetic enough, and it is not - by an enormous margin.

**The numbers.** Microwaves occupy roughly \(\lambda \approx 1\) mm to \(1\) m, that is \(\nu \approx 3 \times 10^{8}\) Hz to \(3 \times 10^{11}\) Hz. Hence

\(E = h\nu \approx (6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8}) = 1.99 \times 10^{-25}\) J \(= 1.24 \times 10^{-6}\) eV  (at the long-wavelength end)

\(E = h\nu \approx (6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{11}) = 1.99 \times 10^{-22}\) J \(= 1.24 \times 10^{-3}\) eV  (at the short-wavelength end)

The **smallest** work function in Table 14.1 is that of potassium, \(2.3\) eV. So even the most energetic microwave photon falls short by a factor of about \(1850\), and the least energetic by a factor of nearly \(2 \times 10^{6}\).

**The chapter's own anchor.** Example 14.2(b) works out the photon energy of an FM radio wave of frequency \(98.3\) MHz as \(6.63 \times 10^{-26}\) J \(= 40.74 \times 10^{-8}\) eV, and remarks that this "is very small energy as compared to the photon energy in the visible range". A microwave photon belongs to the same feeble class. By contrast, Section 14.2.1 states that the source used in the experiment must be of sufficiently high frequency, of **short wavelength \(\le 10^{-7}\) m** - and microwaves are \(10^{4}\) to \(10^{7}\) times longer than that.

**Turning up the power does not help.** In the photon picture, raising the intensity only increases the *number* of photons arriving per second; the energy of each photon is fixed at \(h\nu\) and does not depend on intensity. A million feeble photons cannot be pooled to eject one electron, because each electron absorbs one photon in a single collision. So no matter how powerful the microwave source, the photocurrent stays exactly zero.

*(Note: the chapter lists microwaves among the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in Section 14.1 but does not itself tabulate their wavelength range; the range quoted above is the standard microwave band, which the "Try this" box on page 311 asks the student to chart.)*

**No, it is not always possible - and for every metal listed in Table 14.1 it is not possible at all.**

Photoemission requires \(h\nu \ge \phi_0\), or equivalently \(\lambda \le \lambda_0 = hc/\phi_0\). Whether red light works therefore depends entirely on the work function of the emitter.

**Energy of a red photon.** The chapter computes this in Example 14.2(a) for red light of \(7000\ \mathring{A}\):

\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{7000 \times 10^{-10}} = 2.84 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 1.776\) eV

Across the whole red band (about \(6200\ \mathring{A}\) to \(7500\ \mathring{A}\)) the photon energy runs only from about \(2.0\) eV down to about \(1.66\) eV.

**Compare with Table 14.1.** The smallest work function there is potassium at \(2.3\) eV. So a red photon falls short even for the most easily emitting metal in the table, and falls very far short for gold (\(5.1\) eV). Not a single photoelectron is emitted, and raising the intensity cannot rescue it - that only sends more photons, each still carrying the same insufficient \(1.8\) eV.

**The same statement as a wavelength.** For potassium,

\(\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\phi_0} = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{2.3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 5.4 \times 10^{-7}\) m \(\approx 5400\ \mathring{A}\)

which lies in the **green** part of the visible spectrum. Red light, at \(6200\)-\(7500\ \mathring{A}\), is well beyond this threshold. This is exactly the point of the "Can you tell?" question on page 314: if a cathode fails to respond to green light, only the shorter-wavelength colours (blue, violet) can possibly generate a photocurrent - never red.

**Conclusion.** Red light could produce photoelectric emission only from a photosensitive surface whose work function is below about \(1.8\) eV. No such metal appears in Table 14.1, so with these emitters the answer is a definite no. The general answer to the question as asked is therefore **no - it is never guaranteed**; it depends on the emitter material, and for the common metals red light is simply too feeble.

**Gold**, whose work function is \(5.1\) eV - the largest value in Table 14.1.

**Reasoning.** Photoelectric emission begins only when the photon energy equals the work function, \(h\nu_0 = \phi_0\), so the threshold frequency of a metal is

\(\nu_0 = \dfrac{\phi_0}{h}\)

Since \(h\) is the same universal constant for every metal, \(\nu_0\) is **directly proportional to \(\phi_0\)**. The metal needing the highest incident frequency is therefore simply the metal with the highest work function, and reading down the second column of Table 14.1 that is gold at \(5.1\) eV (nickel is next at \(5.0\) eV; silver and aluminum tie at \(4.3\) eV; potassium is the smallest at \(2.3\) eV).

**The threshold for gold.**

\(\nu_0 = \dfrac{5.1 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{6.63 \times 10^{-34}} = 1.23 \times 10^{15}\) Hz

\(\lambda_0 = \dfrac{c}{\nu_0} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{1.23 \times 10^{15}} = 2.44 \times 10^{-7}\) m \(\approx 2440\ \mathring{A}\)

So gold needs **ultraviolet** radiation; nothing in the visible range will generate a photocurrent from it.

**For contrast**, potassium at the other end of the table needs only

\(\nu_0 = \dfrac{2.3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{6.63 \times 10^{-34}} = 5.55 \times 10^{14}\) Hz, i.e. \(\lambda_0 \approx 5400\ \mathring{A}\)

which is green light. This is why the chapter says that for zinc, cadmium and magnesium ultraviolet radiation is necessary while for alkali metals even visible radiation is sufficient - and why potassium, not gold, is the sensible cathode material for a photocell that must work in ordinary daylight.

**What the term means.** Some experiments can be explained only by treating radiation as a **wave** - interference, diffraction and polarization of light are of this kind. Other experiments can be explained only by treating it as a stream of **particles** - the photoelectric effect and black body radiation need radiation to consist of photons, each carrying a definite quantum of energy \(E = h\nu\), and Compton's scattering of X-rays showed that a photon also carries momentum \(p = E/c = h/\lambda\), like a particle. Some phenomena can be explained by both pictures. Neither model on its own is sufficient, so both characters must be accepted as holding good, **one dominating in some situations and the other working in the rest of the situations**. This double character is what is called **wave-particle duality**.

**Where it applies.** It applies in two places.

1. **To radiation.** Not only to visible light but to the whole electromagnetic spectrum. This is the *wave-particle duality of electromagnetic radiation* (Section 14.3).
2. **To matter.** In 1924 de Broglie argued from the symmetry existing in nature that if radiation has a dual nature then matter may possess one too, and proposed that a moving material particle has a wave associated with it of wavelength \(\lambda = h/p\). Davisson and Germer confirmed this experimentally by obtaining an electron diffraction pattern from a nickel crystal. This is the *wave-particle duality of matter* (Section 14.7).

Taken together, duality implies that **all moving particles have an associated frequency and an associated wave number, and all waves have an associated energy and an associated momentum.**

**Where it is actually observable.** Duality shows itself only on the microscopic scale - we meet the wave-particle duality of matter, due to quantum behaviour, when dealing with objects of size \(\le 10^{-6}\) m. The very small magnitude of \(h\) is what sets that scale. For everyday bodies the associated wavelength is unmeasurably small: Example 14.5 gives \(6.63 \times 10^{-36}\) m for a running student and \(3.32 \times 10^{-38}\) m for a car, both utterly negligible compared with the widths of the paths along which they move, which is why we never notice any wave behaviour in them. In the same way the wave nature of light becomes evident only when the slit width or the separation between slits is comparable to or smaller than the wavelength of the light.

**The derivation.** Einstein's photoelectric equation gives the maximum kinetic energy of an emitted electron as

\(KE_{max} = h\nu - \phi_0\)   ... (14.2)

At the stopping potential \(V_0\) the most energetic electron just fails to reach the collector, i.e. it loses all its kinetic energy in overcoming the retarding field, so \(KE_{max} = eV_0\). Substituting,

\(eV_0 = h\nu - \phi_0\)  or  \(V_0 = \left(\dfrac{h}{e}\right)\nu - \dfrac{\phi_0}{e}\)   ... (14.3)

Now the incident radiation is usually specified by its wavelength rather than its frequency, and \(\lambda\nu = c\), so \(\nu = c/\lambda\). Putting this into (14.3),

\(V_0 = \left(\dfrac{hc}{e}\right)\dfrac{1}{\lambda} - \dfrac{\phi_0}{e}\)

**This is the inverse linear dependence.** \(V_0\) is a **straight line in \(1/\lambda\)**, not in \(\lambda\) - that is, it depends on the *reciprocal* of the wavelength, and does so linearly.

- The **slope** is \(hc/e = 1.24 \times 10^{-6}\) V m. It is built only out of universal constants, so it is the **same for every emitter material** - which is why the lines drawn for different metals in Fig. 14.6 are parallel.
- The **intercept** is \(-\phi_0/e\). This is the only place the emitter material enters, so the intercepts differ from metal to metal.

**Why physically.** A shorter wavelength means a higher frequency, hence a more energetic photon. The electron must always pay the same fixed toll \(\phi_0\) to escape the surface, so the more energetic the photon, the more energy is left over as kinetic energy, and the larger the retarding potential needed to turn the electron back. As \(\lambda\) is increased the photon energy falls, \(V_0\) falls with it, and \(V_0\) reaches zero at the threshold wavelength \(\lambda_0 = hc/\phi_0\). Beyond \(\lambda_0\) there is no emission at all, so the straight line simply stops there.

**A worked illustration** (potassium, \(\phi_0 = 2.3\) eV):

| \(\lambda\) (in \(\mathring{A}\)) | \(1/\lambda\) (per m) | \(V_0\) (in V) |
|---|---|---|
| 4000 | \(2.50 \times 10^{6}\) | 0.81 |
| 5000 | \(2.00 \times 10^{6}\) | 0.19 |
| 5405 | \(1.85 \times 10^{6}\) | 0 |

Notice that \(V_0\) is **not** proportional to \(1/\lambda\) - going from \(5000\ \mathring{A}\) to \(4000\ \mathring{A}\) raises \(1/\lambda\) by only \(25\%\) but raises \(V_0\) more than fourfold. That is the effect of the constant offset \(-\phi_0/e\). It is the *graph* of \(V_0\) against \(1/\lambda\) that is a straight line, and its intercept on the \(1/\lambda\) axis marks the threshold beyond which the photocurrent disappears.

Finally, note that neither the slope nor the intercept contains the intensity: \(V_0\) depends on the incident frequency and on the emitter material, and not at all on how bright the source is.

**The extra energy is not lost. It goes into ejecting a proportionately larger number of photoelectrons - that is, into a larger photocurrent - instead of giving more energy to each electron.**

**Why the maximum kinetic energy cannot change.** In the photon picture the intensity of a beam of a given wavelength is fixed by the **number of photons** falling on unit area in unit time, and not by the energy of an individual photon. Every photon of that wavelength carries exactly \(E = h\nu = hc/\lambda\), whatever the intensity of the beam. The photoelectric process is a one-to-one collision: a photon arrives at the surface, gives **all** of its energy to a single electron, and ceases to exist. That electron spends \(\phi_0\) in escaping and keeps at most the remainder, so

\(KE_{max} = h\nu - \phi_0\)   ... (14.2)

Both terms on the right are fixed - \(h\nu\) by the wavelength of the source and \(\phi_0\) by the emitter material - so \(KE_{max}\) cannot depend on intensity. Doubling the brightness does not make a single photon more energetic; it only makes photons more numerous.

**Where the energy actually goes.** If the intensity is doubled at the same wavelength, twice as many photons strike the surface each second, so twice as many electrons are knocked out each second. The number of emitted electrons - and hence the saturation current \(I_0\) - doubles with it. This is precisely observation 5 of Section 14.2.2 and the linear graph of Fig. 14.3: the photocurrent increases linearly with intensity. So the additional incident energy is fully accounted for; it is **shared among more electrons rather than concentrated on each one**, and energy is conserved throughout.

(Not every extra photon necessarily liberates an electron that reaches the collector - some electrons are ejected from varying depths inside the metal and suffer collisions on the way out, losing part of their energy. But that energy is transferred to the metal, not destroyed.)

**The contrast with wave theory.** This is exactly the observation the wave picture could not survive. On the wave theory, larger intensity means larger energy incident on the surface, so electrons ought to have been emitted with larger kinetic energies and \(KE_{max}\) ought to have risen with intensity. The experiment showed the opposite: \(KE_{max}\) is completely independent of intensity and depends only on the incident frequency. Einstein's quantization of energy resolves this at once, because it separates the two roles - **frequency fixes the energy per electron, intensity fixes the number of electrons.**

**The de Broglie wavelength of an electron.** In 1924 de Broglie argued, from the symmetry existing in nature, that since radiation has a dual nature - sometimes wave-like, sometimes particle-like - matter may possess a dual nature too. He proposed that a **moving** material particle of momentum \(p\) has a wave associated with it, analogous to the wave associated with a photon, whose wavelength is given by the same relation:

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv}\)   ... (14.6)

These waves associated with material particles are called **matter waves**, and \(\lambda\) is the **de Broglie wavelength**. For an electron of mass \(m_e\) moving with speed \(v\), the de Broglie wavelength is \(\lambda = h/(m_e v)\). The greater the momentum, the shorter the wavelength.

If the electron has been accelerated from rest through a potential difference \(V\), the work done \(eV\) becomes its kinetic energy, so \(p = \sqrt{2m_e eV}\) and

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m_e eV}} = \dfrac{1.228}{\sqrt{V \text{ (in volts)}}}\) nm   ... (14.7)

For an electron of energy a few eV this comes to a few \(\mathring{A}\) - for example \(0.112\) nm at \(120\) V. This is not a mere piece of algebra: because that wavelength is of the same order as the spacing of atoms in a crystal, the electron's wave nature can actually be displayed, and Davisson and Germer did so, measuring \(0.165\) nm for \(54\) V electrons against the \(0.167\) nm predicted by Eq. (14.7).

**Will an electron at rest have an associated de Broglie wavelength?**

**No.** An electron at rest has **no** de Broglie wavelength.

**Justification.** For an electron at rest \(v = 0\), so its momentum is

\(p = m_e v = 0\)

and Eq. (14.6) gives

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{0}\)

which is not a finite quantity. As the speed is made smaller and smaller the wavelength grows without any bound, and at \(v = 0\) exactly it is undefined. There is no wave of any definite wavelength to speak of.

This is consistent with the way the hypothesis is stated throughout the chapter. De Broglie's proposal is made for a **moving** material particle, and Section 14.7 puts it in the same terms: wave-particle duality implies that **all moving particles** have an associated frequency and an associated wave number. A stationary particle simply falls outside the relation.

Put physically: the wave is associated with the particle *because* the particle carries momentum. With zero momentum there is nothing for \(\lambda = h/p\) to fix, and so no matter wave exists.

The importance of the Davisson and Germer experiment (1927) is that it converted de Broglie's hypothesis from a proposal into an experimentally established fact. Specifically:

**1. It gave the first direct experimental confirmation of the wave nature of a material particle.** A beam of electrons from an electron gun was accelerated, collimated and made to fall on a nickel crystal, and the intensity of the scattered electrons was measured with a movable detector as the scattering angle \(\theta\) was varied. The scattered intensity was **not** uniform in all directions, as classical theory predicted it should be. Instead the pattern showed peaks, corresponding to constructive interference, and troughs, corresponding to destructive interference - that is, a **diffraction pattern**. Diffraction is a property of waves, so electrons scattered from the crystal must be behaving as waves.

**2. It verified de Broglie's relation quantitatively, not merely qualitatively.** Varying the accelerating potential from \(44\) V to \(68\) V, they found a peak in the scattered intensity at a scattering angle of \(50^\circ\) for a potential of \(54\) V. The de Broglie relation, Eq. (14.7), predicts

\(\lambda = \dfrac{1.228}{\sqrt{54}} = 0.167\) nm

while the wavelength deduced from the electron diffraction measurements was \(0.165\) nm. The theoretical and experimental values were in close agreement, so \(\lambda = h/p\) was confirmed as a correct numerical law and not just a plausible analogy.

**3. It extended wave-particle duality from radiation to matter.** Before this, duality was a statement about light and about the electromagnetic spectrum. The Davisson and Germer experiment substantiated de Broglie's hypothesis of wave-particle duality for material particles and verified his relation, establishing that a particle of matter shows wave behaviour under suitable conditions. G. P. Thomson reached the same conclusion independently in England in 1928 by diffracting electrons through metals.

**Why a crystal had to be used.** The wavelength associated with an electron of a few eV is only of the order of a few \(\mathring{A}\). To observe wave behaviour, the diffracting object must be of the same order of magnitude - and the atoms of a crystal, with a spacing of a few \(\mathring{A}\), are exactly that. The peak observed was the result of constructive interference of electrons scattered from the different layers of the regularly spaced atoms of the nickel crystal. Nothing of coarser scale would have revealed the effect.

**Recognition.** The significance of this line of work was marked by two Nobel prizes in Physics: de Broglie in 1929, and Davisson, Germer and Thomson in 1937. As the chapter notes, it is remarkable that Sir J. J. Thomson discovered the electron as a sub-atomic **particle** while his son G. P. Thomson showed that the electron behaves like a **wave**.
